newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU fears EMU woes may gatecrash Amsterdam summit.
newsitem.headline: EU fears EMU woes may gatecrash Amsterdam summit.

text.p: Europe's white-knuckle ride towards monetary union threatens to spill over into a European Union summit in Amsterdam in two weeks.

The summit, to be held in the confines of the Dutch Central Bank building, was supposed to be a largely EMU-free zone, focusing on the nitty-gritty of internal EU reforms in a new treaty to prepare the 15-member bloc for its ambitious eastward expansion.

But the recent furore over German plans to revalue gold assets in a desperate bid to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) and the election in France of a Socialist government that has vowed to review European policy have raised serious doubts over the prospects for a credible single currency.

As the Union moves into a crucial phase on both EMU and the treaty, financial markets say that France and Germany's problems in qualifying for EMU give the bloc a stark choice -- launch a weak euro on time or delay the project.
Either way, the credibility of the bloc and its new currency could be severely dented.

The June 16-17 summit agenda, dominated by issues as esoteric as subsidiarity, flexibility and transparency, does also require agreement on the legal framework of monetary union's Stability Pact, agreed at last December's Dublin summit.

French premier Lionel Jospin, who campaigned by opposing an austerity programme launched to help France meet EMU criteria, had said that he would re-open the debate on the pact, but analysts wonder how committed Paris is to rewriting the deal.

Politically, EU diplomats say it is difficult to see how the bloc would reopen talks on the pact, which sets stiff fines for EMU governments with excessive deficits, adding that debate is more likely to focus on addressing France's concerns on jobs.
Diplomats remain adamant that summit leaders will not allow monetary union woes to derail efforts to sign a new treaty.
"Everybody wants to get this out of the way," one said, one said of the inter-governmental conference (IGC) treaty review.
"Certainly EMU will be overhanging the summit, but they're very determined to get through the IGC...they've got a lot to do, more than they had to do at Maastricht."
But they admit that the fact the summit is being held unusally on a Monday and Tuesday, when financial markets will be open, could create an unwanted diversion from the IGC issue.
"Because finance ministers will be in Amsterdam, and because markets will be open, EMU is an issue that won't be allowed to go away and (that) could create a difficulty," one said.

Diplomats said that the summit, aware of keen market interest in financial issues rather than the uninspiring IGC, would probably use an agreement on the stability pact and choose a design for the new euro coin as a signal that they were committed to keeping EMU on track.
"They wouldn't be taken seriously if they let EMU hijack their agenda. But, if they put it up the agenda, everyone would smell a crisis," the diplomat said.
Another said that the summit's priority was to finalise the IGC talks so as to be able to concentrate on other pressing issues, such as monetary union, during the rest of the year.

They said EU finance ministers, meeting in Luxembourg next Sunday and Monday to discuss outstanding EMU issues including the pact and the post-EMU exchange rate mechanism, would probably try and head off any EMU problems before Amsterdam.
One diplomat joked that once EU leaders had chosen a new euro coin, they could at least toss it to see whether or not to go ahead with the project.
